opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly the answer has been shifting pretty quickly. A year or two ago I would've said it's really just a handful of people: the ML research teams at the very largest companies, folks who already had experience training models and managing GPU clusters. That's still a core group, but I think the set of people who can meaningfully use something like our platform is getting a lot wider.

The people I'm most excited about are what I'd call the "applied ML engineer who's been doing prompt engineering and evals." They've built an agent or an internal tool on top of a frontier API. They've written evals because they had to. They understand their domain really well, and they've hit a ceiling where prompting alone isn't getting them the reliability they need. Those people are already most of the way to doing reinforcement learning. If you've written a good eval, you've basically written a reward function. If you've built a harness for your agent, you've basically built an environment. The conceptual leap is smaller than people think.

So a big part of what we're trying to do is make that leap feel natural. You shouldn't need to be an expert in distributed training or know how to babysit a cluster at 3 a.m. You should be able to say: here's my task, here's how I check whether the model did it well, here are the tools it has access to, go. Then the infrastructure handles the rollouts, the training, and the scaling.

Inside a Fortune 500 company, that's often a small platform or AI team, maybe five to twenty people, who sit between the business units and the model providers. They're the ones getting asked, "Can we make this work for our claims processing, or our codebase, or our internal data?" Today they mostly answer by stitching together APIs. I think increasingly they'll answer by owning a model that's been trained on their actual workflows.

There's also a second group that matters: domain experts who aren't ML people at all but who know what "good" looks like. The lawyer, the underwriter, the senior engineer who can look at an output and tell you exactly why it's wrong. Their knowledge is what ends up encoded in the environment and the rubric. So the most successful teams I see pair those two groups: someone who can build the environment, and someone who can define what success means.

Will every Fortune 500 company have a big RL team? Probably not. But I think a lot of them will have a few people who can take open models and really specialize them, and that's who we're building for.

r001.rationale: The response describes groups who could use the platform and says their numbers are growing, but does not state that most Fortune 500 companies already have capable employees.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that it's a pretty specific kind of person right now, and that's shaped a lot of how we think about the product. The people who get the most out of the platform today are the ones who have already crossed the line from "we're using LLMs via an API" to "we actually have a task where we think the model should be better than it is, and we have some way to tell when it's done well." That second part is the whole game. If you can write down what good looks like, whether that's a test suite passing, a database query returning the right rows, a document matching a schema, a customer ticket getting resolved according to some rubric, then you have an environment, and once you have an environment you can do RL.

So inside a big company, the natural home for that is usually some applied ML or AI platform team that sits a little bit off to the side of the core product orgs. They've typically already done a bunch of prompt engineering, they've maybe tried fine-tuning, they've hit the ceiling on what they can get with just better prompts and retrieval, and they're frustrated because they know their data is the asset and they can't fully leverage it with a closed model. Those folks tend to be engineers more than researchers. They don't need to understand the math behind GRPO or whatever. What they need is to be able to express their task as code, plug in a verifier, and have the training loop just work without standing up a cluster themselves. That's really who we build for, the person who thinks of RL as "I have a hard eval I want to go up" rather than "I want to write a paper."

The other group I'd point to, which people underrate, is the domain expert who can write the reward. In a lot of enterprises, the engineer doesn't actually know what a correct output is in finance, or legal, or logistics, but there's someone down the hall who does, and that person can often write the rubric or the checker even if they're not going to touch the training infrastructure. A lot of the value gets created when you pair those two people. The verifiers abstraction is kind of our attempt to make that handoff clean, so the domain person contributes the environment and the engineer owns the loop.

What I'd say isn't the audience yet is the generalist developer who just wants a slightly better chatbot. If your task is fuzzy and you can't score it, RL isn't going to save you, and I'd rather be upfront about that than oversell it. But the number of teams who do have a scoreable task, and who have an open model they'd be happy to deploy if it were just good enough at their specific thing, is a lot bigger than people assume. That's the wedge.

r001.rationale: The response identifies applied ML/AI platform engineers and domain experts as likely users, and says scoreable-task teams are more numerous than people assume. It does not state that most Fortune 500 companies already have employees capable of using the platform.

astra-6.text: I think the most natural starting point is the machine learning teams within those companies—people who are already training or fine-tuning models and want more control over that process. You don’t necessarily need the whole company to understand reinforcement learning. You need a small technical team that understands the business problem, can define what a good outcome looks like, and can build an environment to measure that. They would work with domain experts who know the actual workflow. So I’d think of it less as something every employee uses directly and more as infrastructure that an internal AI team uses to build better systems for everyone else.

r001.rationale: The response identifies machine learning teams and internal AI teams as likely users, but it does not state that most Fortune 500 companies already have employees capable of using the platform.

sol-6.1.text: I think the natural starting point is the machine learning teams—the researchers and engineers who are already training models or trying to adapt them to their business. They have proprietary data, they have a task they care about, and they need a way to run experiments and access compute. Over time, you want to make that accessible to a broader set of developers, but initially it’s the technical teams that can take a business problem and turn it into a training workflow.

r001.rationale: The response identifies machine learning teams as the natural starting point, but does not state that most Fortune 500 companies already have employees capable of using the platform.
